topic: Delhi HC: a paying guest (PG) arrangement is closer to a licence than a lease - the PG operator keeps overall control and the occupant only gets permission to use a room or bed, so the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 does not protect a PG occupant; once the licence is terminated the occupant must vacate (Sant Lal Jain v. Avtar Singh); occupant who entered through the operator cannot dispute her title (Section 122 BSA, earlier Section 116 Evidence Act); unregistered plain-paper agreement to buy rooms gives no right to stay; possession decree on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC upheld, second appeal dismissed (Payal v. Pooja Gupta, RSA 166/2026, 2026:DHC:10313, Justice Neena Bansal Krishna, 20 Nov 2026, reported 23-24 Nov 2026)

slides.title: Living in a PG? You are **not a tenant**.
slides.subtitle: A paying guest gets **permission to use** a room or bed, not a lease. So rent control law does not protect a PG stay.
slides.cite: **Payal v. Pooja Gupta** · RSA 166/2026 · 2026:DHC:10313 · Justice Neena Bansal Krishna · 20 November 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: One bed, then a **long fight**
bullets: A woman ran a **PG for girl students and working women** in Shakarpur, Delhi. In **November 2021**, a resident was given one bed in a shared room.
The operator said the resident stopped paying from **January 2023**, quarrelled with others and refused to leave after the arrangement was **ended by notice**.
The resident claimed she was a **tenant** and had paid **Rs 2 lakh** to buy two rooms under a **plain-paper agreement**.

slides.label: What the Court said
slides.title: A PG is a **licence**
bullets: A **lease** gives the tenant an interest in the property. A **licence** only gives permission to use it.
In a PG, the operator keeps **overall control and management**. The resident only uses a room or bed. So it is closer to a **licence**.
That means the **Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958** does not apply. Once the licence is ended, the resident has to **vacate**.
slides.note: **Law fact:** A person who got in through someone cannot later deny that person's right to the property (**Section 122, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam**).

slides.label: The paper deal
slides.title: Unregistered paper, **no right to stay**
bullets: Her stay began **before** the plain-paper agreement, and that paper did not change why she was living there.
Even if it was an agreement to buy, an **unregistered** paper gives **no right to keep occupying** the rooms. She can pursue a separate case on it.
Result: the order to hand back possession was **upheld** and her appeal was **dismissed**.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: What this ruling **does not** mean
bullets: It does **not** mean every rented flat or room is a licence. Courts look at the **real nature** of the arrangement, not just its label.
Here the operator **went to court** and got a possession order. Keep **receipts and written terms** for any PG stay.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Staying in a PG? The Delhi High Court says you are a licensee, not a tenant 🏠⚖️

A woman ran a PG for girl students and working women in Shakarpur, Delhi. A resident given one bed in a shared room in 2021 allegedly stopped paying, quarrelled with others and refused to leave after the arrangement was ended. She said she was a tenant and had paid Rs 2 lakh to buy two rooms under a plain-paper agreement.

Justice Neena Bansal Krishna explained that a lease gives a person an interest in the property, while a licence only gives permission to use it. In a PG, the operator keeps overall control, so the arrangement is closer to a licence. The Delhi Rent Control Act does not protect it, and once the licence is ended, the resident must vacate.

The Court also said an unregistered plain-paper agreement to buy does not give a right to keep living there, though she can pursue a separate case on it. The possession order was upheld and her appeal dismissed. Remember, courts look at the real nature of each arrangement, so not every rented room is a licence.

Case: Payal v. Pooja Gupta, RSA 166/2026, 2026:DHC:10313
Court: Delhi High Court, Justice Neena Bansal Krishna (20 November 2026)
